summary: Russia issues a unified 30-day eVisa to citizens of the 65 countries and territories on the Foreign Ministry's e-visa list (as of 8 October 2026), including all 27 EU member states, admits CIS neighbors and much of Latin America and the Gulf visa-free, and requires an embassy visa from US, UK, Canadian and Australian travelers. Note that the UK Foreign Office advises against all travel to Russia and Canada says to avoid all travel.

currencyLimits.text: The UK Foreign Office says you may bring cash in any currency and travellers' cheques into or out of Russia without declaring them if their combined value does not exceed the equivalent of USD 10,000, and that you cannot leave Russia with more than that, even if you complete a customs declaration.

source.name: UK FCDO — Russia travel advice, entry requirements

notes: The UK Foreign Office says you must complete a customs declaration for goods worth more than 10,000 US dollars, and for items of cultural or historical significance, rare plants or animals, vehicles, weapons, and medicines containing potent, toxic or psychoactive substances, whatever their value.

The UK Foreign Office says you need a licence before travelling with certain electronic equipment, including GPS devices, and that the number of electronic items for personal use is limited, and that using a drone requires permission from the Russian aviation authority.
The UK Foreign Office says cannabidiol (CBD) is illegal in Russia, even in products bought legally elsewhere, and that exporting antiques or artwork without a Ministry of Culture permit is illegal.

payments.text: The UK Foreign Office says Mastercard and Visa are not operating in Russia: cards issued outside Russia will not work in shops or ATMs, while cards issued inside Russia work only there. Paying in foreign currency is illegal; to buy roubles, take US dollars or euros and change them only at banks, hotels and exchange bureaus.

safety.text: The UK Foreign Office advises against all travel to Russia and Canada says to avoid all travel. The FCDO cites drone attacks and air-defence activity, a lack of flights, very limited consular support, an increased risk of detention and a high likelihood of terrorist attacks, including in major cities. It says British-Russian dual nationals are treated as Russian citizens, and that people whose draft notice appears on the electronic register cannot leave Russia.

tips.text: The UK Foreign Office advises against all travel to Russia, citing drone attacks and air-defence activity, the lack of flights and limited consular support, and Canada says to avoid all travel. The FCDO says Russian authorities treat British-Russian dual nationals as Russian citizens, which limits the consular help the UK can give.

The UK Foreign Office says Mastercard and Visa cards issued outside Russia will not work in Russian shops or ATMs. To buy roubles, take US dollars or euros and change them only at banks, hotels and exchange bureaus; changing money with street traders is illegal.
The unified eVisa is single-entry, valid 120 days for a stay of up to 30 days, and only usable at the approved border crossings listed on evisa.kdmid.ru.

The UK Foreign Office says you must register with the local authorities if you stay anywhere for more than 7 working days, that hotels do this automatically, and that if you cannot show your registration and passport you may be detained for up to 48 hours for identity checks or fined.

The UK Foreign Office reports drone attacks and explosions particularly near the Russian border with Ukraine, says terrorists are active in the North Caucasus, and says access to military and border zones is restricted without permission from local authorities.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Russia?
faq.answer: Most travelers do. Citizens of the 65 countries and territories on the Foreign Ministry's e-visa list (as of 8 October 2026) — including all 27 EU states, India, Japan and several Gulf monarchies — can use the unified 30-day eVisa, while CIS neighbors, much of Latin America and a handful of bilateral partners enter visa-free. US, UK, Canadian, Australian and New Zealand citizens must obtain a visa from a Russian consulate.

faq.question: Can US or UK citizens get the Russian eVisa?
faq.answer: No. The United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia and New Zealand are not on the eVisa eligibility list, so their citizens need a visa from a Russian consulate; for a tourist visa the consulate asks for a confirmation from a registered tour operator or a hotel booking.

faq.question: How does the Russian unified eVisa work?
faq.answer: You apply and pay online at evisa.kdmid.ru. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs says a fee is charged, paid by bank card and not refunded, and that children under six pay no consular fee; it does not publish the amount. Applications are processed in no more than four calendar days. The visa is single-entry, valid for 120 days from issue, allows a stay of up to 30 days, and can only be used at approved border crossings.

faq.question: Is it safe to travel to Russia right now?
faq.answer: The UK Foreign Office advises against all travel to Russia and Canada says to avoid all travel. The FCDO cites drone attacks and air-defence activity, a lack of flights, very limited consular support, an increased risk of detention, and a high likelihood that terrorists will try to carry out attacks, including in major cities.

faq.question: Can I pay by card in Russia?
faq.answer: Not with a card issued abroad. The UK Foreign Office says Mastercard and Visa are not operating in Russia, so cards issued outside Russia will not work in shops or ATMs. Bring US dollars or euros to exchange for roubles at banks, hotels or exchange bureaus.

faq.question: Do I need to register my stay in Russia?
faq.answer: The UK Foreign Office says you must register with the local authorities if you stay anywhere for more than 7 working days. It says hotels do this automatically, that if you stay with someone you should check that they do it, and that you must show evidence of your registration at passport control when you leave Russia.
